title: Early Sparta
author: Ancient
content:
Early Sparta

How Sparta dealt with overpopulation and land hunger

A.  Taras (Tarentum) was Sparta's only colony. (Fornara, # 9).

	B.  Why?  Spartans resolved land hunger by conquest closer to home. 

		1.  Ancient tradition said the colonists were non-participants in the Mess. Wars

		2.  Or else the offspring of those. Is this believable?  

	C.  Argos to the NW was too strong (Battle of Hysiae, c. 669 ??)

		1.  More on that episode in the hoplite panel (Pheidon).

	D.  A large fertile plain was across the Taygetus range in Messenia.  

The Messenian Wars

A.  Problem of chronology exemplifies one difficulty of early Greek history.

		a.  See Wade-Gery, "The Rhianos-hypothesis" in Ehrenberg Studies, 289-302.

	B.  Epaminondas in 370/69 said he'd liberated Messenia after 230 years.

		a.  Plut. Mor. 194b.

	C.  Ephorus distinguished two Messenian Wars.  FGrH III A Comm. 112-119.

		a.  The first lasted 20 years and ended in Spartan subjugation of Messenia.

		a.  The second began with a Messenian revolt.

	D.  Tyrtaios' poems of exhortation are for a Messenian War.

		a.  Tyrt. fr. 4:  fathers of our fathers fought Messene for 19 years.

	E.  The Olympic victor lists imply a date of 736-716 for the 1st war. 

		a.  See Fornara # 3.  Answer: who is "Eusebius"?

		b.  No Messenians in the Olympic victor lists after 736.  

		c.  Firm date for Taras foundation c. 706 BC.  

	F.  If Tyrtaios is literal, 2nd war cannot postdate c. 650.

	G.  Solutions

		a.  The 20 years war is the only one, and Tyrtaios is not literal.

		b.  Epaminondas calculated wrong.  

		c.  Either way Messenia was definitely subjugated by c. 600.

		d.  Preferred solution: downdate Tyrtaios.  

The Grimness of Life in Laconia

A.  Sealey argues helot condition was not so bad.

		a.  Else how send 7 helots with each Spartiate (Hdt. 9.10.1)?

		b.  Helot condition is at the heart of understanding Spartan society.

		c.  Thuc.  4. 80. 3

	B.  Artistic production counts likewise.  Cook, CQ (1962).

Riddles of the Rhetra (= Plut. Lyc. 6)

A.  Oracular utterance or Spartan Law?

		a.  Probably Spartan Law, with the advice or support of Delphi.

		b.  Plutarch got his text from Aristotle's Politeia.

		c.  Excursus:  the Aristotelian Politeiai.  

	B.  Probouleutic power of the Gerousia.

	C.  Power of the assembly:  confirm or deny.

	D.  Unanswered questions:

		a.  Could any member of the assembly speak?  cf. Thersites

		b.  Could the assembly alter a proposal?  

	E.  Is the Rhetra genuine?  What would "genuine" mean in this context?

		a.  The skeptic's objections:  (see Gagarin Early Gk Law 53 n 9)

			1.  Why the seemingly irrelevant item about tribes and villages (obes)?

				a.  Wade-Gery:  replacing hereditary divisions (3 tribes) with regional ones (5 obes).

				b.  A possible difficulty:  the names of six obes are attested. 

				c.  But only if we assume no change by the Roman period. 

			2.  Why refer to the kings as archagetai (a title for founders of colonies & cults)?

			3.  Why the poetic language (phylas phylaksonta obas obaksonta)?

   		b.  One possible answer:  we have a genuine oracle or orally transmitted passage.

			1.  We saw the oracle with the force of law at Kyrene ??

			2.  Contrast the rider, which sounds like legal language. 

		c.  Tyrtaios fr. 3 = Plut. Lyc. 6.7, seems to confirm that Tyrtaios knew the Rhetra.

			1.  It attests a probouleutic function or two-stage procedure.

			2.  That is decisive in favor of genuineness, e.g. for Wade-Gery.

			3.  But a tradition of probouleusis is attested in various primitive legal systems.

			4.  Examples:  Iliad 2, Early Rome, the Germans as described in the Germania.

		d.  Skeptic (Jeffery, Sealey) says it is not so close to the Rhetra.

			1.  It looks more monarchical.

			2.  It does not mention ephors, but classical sources clearly show their power.

			3.  Motive for forgery:  to weaken the position of some unfriendly ephors.

Powers of the Kings

A.  Declaring Wars?  So Hdt. 6. 56

		a.  But Thuc.'s account of the decision for the Peloponnesian War suggests otherwise.

	B.  Jurisdiction over adoptions, heiresses, roads.

		a.  Adoptions and heiresses show centrality of concern with ethnic purity.

		b.  Roads ??  Probably this means property boundaries.  

	C.  Generalship

Power of the Ephors

 (5 annually, elected by assembly)

	A.  Exchange of oaths with the Kings: X. Rep. Lac. 15.7  

	B.  Chilon, founder of the ephorate 

	C.  Thuc. 1.131, ephors can imprison the king.  

	D.  Ephors conduct the xenelasia (expulsion of foreigners)

	E.  Ephors are the real target of the rider to the rhetra? 
 

Land and Allotments

A.  Under the developed constitution (6th BC on) each Spartiate had an allotment (klaros).

	B.  The traditional number of Spartiates was 9,000 - - hence 9,000 lots (Plut. Lyc. 8).

	C.  Land ownership in feudal societies.

	D.  In 243 BC King Agis proposed a redistribution into 4,500 lots.

		a.  This was after the liberation of Messenia by Epaminondas.

		b.  Maybe there were equal numbers of lots in Messenia and Laconia.

	E.  Civil strife over land is attested in the 7th century (Arist. Pol. 1306b-1307c).

		a.  Aristotle cites Tyrtaeus.  Quoted at Bury-Meiggs p. 524 note 7. 

		b.  Reflects agitation for landed status by newly empowered hoplites?

		c.  Solution A:  no, but it could reflect genuine agitation after 2nd Messenian.

		d.  Solution B:  yes, but we have to have the late dates all the way around.

	F.  Lots are inalienable in Sparta.  

		a.  Inalienability of land is a way to preserve an aristocracy.
